Tucker3 tensor model across strata (three-way Lee-Carter model)

Source: R/model-tucker3.R
tucker3.Rd

Joint model of the array of log rates [age, period, stratum]: the three-way extension of the Lee-Carter model of Russolillo, Giordano and Haberman (2011). Status: published, with the deviations listed below; section and equation numbers refer to that paper.

Usage

tucker3(
  ranks = c(2, 2, 2),
  transform = c("log", "coda"),
  ts = c("rwd", "arima", "ets"),
  residual_noise = FALSE,
  centre = TRUE,
  maxit = 200,
  tol = 1e-08
)

Arguments

ranks

Tucker ranks for age, period and stratum (default c(2, 2, 2), Russolillo et al. 2011, Section 3.2), or "bic" / "aic" to choose them by an information criterion on the training data (package-specific: n log(RSS / n) plus the penalty times the number of parameters of the factor matrices and the core; ranks up to 6 for age and period and up to 4 for strata). For selection by forecast accuracy use tuned().

transform

"log", or the deprecated "coda" (use coda_multiway()).

ts

Forecast method for the period factors: "rwd", "arima", "ets".

residual_noise

Add the in-sample residual variation (per age and stratum, normal on the transformed scale) to the draws. The residuals contain the observation noise of the training years, which predictive draws add again as Poisson variation, so the noise is then counted twice. Default FALSE (earlier development versions: TRUE).

centre

Remove the mean over the years of each age and stratum before the decomposition and add it back afterwards (Russolillo, Giordano and Haberman 2011). With FALSE the decomposition describes the log rates themselves.

maxit, tol

Settings of the HOOI iterations.

Value

A model specification.

Details

Model (Section 2, eq. 7-8). As in Lee-Carter, the mean log rate over the years of each age and stratum, a[x, i], is removed (centre = TRUE), and the centred array is decomposed by a Tucker3 decomposition X - a = G x1 A x2 B x3 C with ranks ranks = c(age, period, stratum): column-wise orthonormal age factors A, period factors B and stratum factors C, linked by the core array G, estimated by least squares. Ranks c(1, 1, 1) give eq. (7), log m[x, t, i] - a[x, i] = b[x] k[t] c[i] (one period index for all strata); the default c(2, 2, 2) is the model of the application (Section 3.2, ten European countries). The squared core elements over the sum of squares of the centred array are the shares of variation of each combination of components (Table 4); their sum is the fit (fit$fits$fit_pct, core_pct).

Forecasts. The paper proposes a time-series model for the period index, as in Lee-Carter, and leaves its form open (Section 3.2.2). Here the period factors (columns of B) follow a multivariate random walk with drift, as k[t] of Lee and Carter (1992); draws resample the joint year-to-year changes, which keeps their correlation, and include the uncertainty of the drift (ts = "rwd"). ARIMA or ETS models per column (ts = "arima", "ets", package forecast) are alternatives. Bergeron-Boucher, Simonacci, Oeppen and Gallo (2018) forecast this model with one component per mode and a random walk with drift of the period index, as tucker3(ranks = c(1, 1, 1)) does; their draws resample the errors of the index and keep the drift fixed. The rates are rebuilt with a, A, C and G fixed. Draws carry the uncertainty of the forecast period factors only. With fewer period factors than independent trends in the data, the strata share their forecast uncertainty and intervals are too narrow: in an example on simulated Lee-Carter data with Poisson deaths and an own random walk in each of 10 strata, 95% intervals covered about 74% with the default ranks and 95% with ranks = c(1, 10, 10). Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates and the exposures, and no other observation noise. If intervals are too narrow on real data, that is a property of the model (see recalibrated(), ensemble(), or overdispersed models such as stanmomo(family = "nb")).

Deviations from the paper.

  • Estimation: the paper fits the model by alternating least squares (footnote 3; Kiers' Tucker3 program for Matlab, Appendix); here by higher-order orthogonal iteration (HOOI; De Lathauwer, De Moor and Vandewalle 2000), an alternating least-squares algorithm for the same criterion. The paper also rotates the solution to simple structure, which leaves the fitted values unchanged; signs are fixed so that the largest entry of each factor is positive.

  • Centring: the text and eq. (7) centre over the years; the Matlab session in the Appendix also centres across the age groups. The package follows eq. (7), because the term removed by centring across ages varies over the years and the paper gives no forecast for it.

  • Package-specific (reference unknown): the forecast model of the period factors (see above), the choice of the ranks by an information criterion (ranks = "bic", "aic"), and the replacement of zero deaths by 0.5 before taking logarithms. The paper's data end with the closed age group 95-99; an open age interval is treated like the other age groups.

Deprecated: transform = "coda" (centred log-ratio transformed life-table deaths in place of log rates) still works and warns (class mt_warning_deprecated). Its forecast of all period factors by a multivariate random walk, its auxiliary random walk for the rate of the open age interval and its 0.5 deaths in empty cells are package-specific. Use coda_multiway(), the published multiway compositional model of Bergeron-Boucher, Simonacci, Oeppen and Gallo (2018), or coda() (coherent = TRUE) for a common component with deviations per stratum.

Ranks are reduced to the array dimensions where needed, so the model also runs with one stratum or one age group. The model is experimental: compare it with established models such as li_lee() in a backtest before using it.

References

Russolillo M, Giordano G, Haberman S (2011). Extending the Lee-Carter model: a three-way decomposition. Scandinavian Actuarial Journal 2011(2): 96-117. doi:10.1080/03461231003611933

Lee RD, Carter LR (1992). Modeling and forecasting U.S. mortality. Journal of the American Statistical Association 87(419): 659-671.

De Lathauwer L, De Moor B, Vandewalle J (2000). On the best rank-1 and rank-(R1, R2, ..., RN) approximation of higher-order tensors. SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications 21(4): 1324-1342. doi:10.1137/S0895479898346995

Kolda TG, Bader BW (2009). Tensor decompositions and applications. SIAM Review 51(3): 455-500. doi:10.1137/07070111X

Bergeron-Boucher M-P, Simonacci V, Oeppen J, Gallo M (2018). Coherent modeling and forecasting of mortality patterns for subpopulations using multiway analysis of compositions: an application to Canadian provinces and territories. North American Actuarial Journal 22(1): 92-118. doi:10.1080/10920277.2017.1377620

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single")
fit <- mt_fit(tucker3(), x)
fit$fits$fit_pct
#> [1] 79.90136
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
